newsitem.title: GERMANY: Summers says dollar in a "very strong position".
newsitem.headline: Summers says dollar in a "very strong position".

text.p: U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said on Tuesday he believed the dollar was "in a very strong position" and that financial markets would be fine if the United States maintained solid fundamentals.

"I believe the dollar is in a very strong position and what is most important for the United States is to maintain sound fundamentals," Summers said from Washington in a video link-up to a panel discussion at the Frankfurt Global 24 conference.
"If we are able to maintain sound fundamentals, as we have done in recent years, then we will be fine," Summers said.

Summers said there was no inflation in sight despite the strong U.S. economy and that the dollar, which he said has a strong position as an international reserve currency, had little to fear from financial developments.
"The dollar share in worldwide reserves has been stable over time, while there will be changes no doubt in financial patterns as different currencies evolve," he said.

"It is important that we maintain the type of capital markets and fundamental polices that make our country attractive to foreign investors," he said. "If we do that, then the dollar has little to fear."
Summers said he did not try to predict financial markets or to interpret the movements of markets, which he said "reflect a wide range of factors."
He cited one factor influencing markets as projections for a lower 1997 budget deficit.

"I think that's a source of success," he said of budget deficit projections. "Low levels of unemployment without any real signs of accelerating inflation are another sign of strengthening fundamentals."
Summers said it was hard to assign any one factor to the movements of the dollar but said one factor, among others, was the run-up to European monetary union, set to begin in 1999.
"I think there are many factors and I have no doubt that perceptions about European financial policies are one variable that affect exchange rates," he said.
"But we regard the most important factor for having a healthy dollar is the maintenance of strong fundamentals at home," he said.
Summers reaffirmed Washington's commitment to Europe, saying "the macroeconomic developments in Europe are of great importance to us."
"Our hope is that it will not divert Europe from other profoundly important changes that its faces, ones that are crucial to the success of monetary policy," he said.
Summers called on Europe to create an economic environment in which barriers to employment creation are improved and flexibility is enhanced.

"Another top priority for Europe is the need for integration across the European continent, which will require the European Union to look to the east, which is very important to us in defining a post cold-war world," he said.
